title: The sky turns
subtitle: Why stars rise, set and circle the pole, and how fast they do it

sections.heading: One sky, turning as a piece
body: After this lesson you will be able to look at any star and say where it will be in an hour, and you will know why the chart you learned at 8 pm looks tilted at midnight.

Go out twice on the same night, an hour apart, and the stars have moved. They have not moved against each other: the constellations keep their shapes. The whole sky has turned as one piece, like a picture painted on the inside of a dome. The dome is not really turning. You are. Earth spins once a day from west to east, so everything in the sky appears to drift the other way, from east to west.

demo.title: Facing north with the clock running

steps.caption: Facing north at 8 pm in mid-January. Polaris stands as many degrees above the horizon as the latitude you are watching from. The Big Dipper stands on its handle, low in the north-northeast.
Now time runs at half an hour per second. Everything wheels counter-clockwise around Polaris, which hardly moves. The dots mark the Dipper star Dubhe once an hour until dawn: each gap is 15° of turn.

1 am, five hours later. Dubhe has swung 75° around the pole, from the lower right of Polaris to the upper right, and the whole Dipper is high in the northeast. Dubhe never leaves this circle, day or night.

The southern hemisphere's version: facing south from mid-southern latitudes (34°S) on the same evening, an hour per second. Here the sky wheels clockwise around the south celestial pole, an empty-looking spot 34° up. The Southern Cross and the two Pointers swing around it and never set.

figures.caption: Earth spins inside a sphere of stars. Press Spin Earth: the stars never move, but your horizon (green) tips across them, so stars come up over it in the east and drop below it in the west.

misconception.myth: The stars move across the sky on their own during the night.
misconception.fact: The stars keep their places, relative to each other and to us. It is Earth that turns, once a day from west to east, so everything in the sky, the Sun and Moon included, appears to drift the other way, east to west, at the same steady rate.

check.prompt: In the figure the stars stay put while your horizon tips across them. What is actually turning?
choices: The sphere of stars, once a day
Earth, once a day
The Sun, carrying the stars with it
Nothing: each star drifts on its own
check.explanation: Earth spins on its axis once a day. Standing on it, you see the whole sky appear to turn the opposite way.

sections.heading: The pivot and the speed
body: The still point of the turning sky is a celestial pole, the spot directly above one of Earth's poles. In the northern hemisphere it is the north celestial pole, and [[star:Polaris|Polaris]] happens to sit less than 1° from it, which is why it stays put while everything else circles; facing north, the motion is counter-clockwise. In the southern hemisphere the pivot is the south celestial pole, which has no bright star to mark it; facing south, the motion is clockwise. From {{place}} your pivot is the {{pole}}.

The speed is easy to remember: a full turn of 360° in 24 hours is 15° per hour. A fist held at arm's length covers about 10°, so in one hour a star moves a fist and a half along its circle. Stars close to the pole trace small circles and seem to crawl; stars far from it sweep long arcs across the sky, but all of them turn through the same 15° each hour.

figures.caption: With the shutter open, every star draws an arc around the celestial pole. Slide the exposure: each hour adds 15° to every trail, short or long, because the whole sky turns as one piece.

image.alt: Long-exposure photograph of the Gemini North telescope dome under concentric star trails circling the north celestial pole.

figures.caption: A real long exposure over Maunakea, Hawaii. Every trail is part of a circle around one still point, the north celestial pole; the trails near it are short and tight, the ones far from it long and sweeping, yet all span the same angle.

misconception.myth: Polaris, the North Star, is the brightest star in the sky.
misconception.fact: Polaris is an ordinary second-magnitude star, roughly the 50th brightest, and city haze can hide it. It is famous for where it is, less than 1° from the north celestial pole, not for how bright it is. The brightest star at night is Sirius.

thinkAbout.question: In one hour, a star 60° from the pole and a star 10° from the pole both turn with the sky. Which one travels farther across the sky, and which one turns through the bigger angle?
thinkAbout.answer: The star 60° out sweeps an arc about five times longer across the sky, but both turn through the same 15° around the pole. That is why every trail in a long exposure spans the same angle: short and tight near the pole, long and sweeping far from it.

sections.heading: Rising in the east, setting in the west
body: Turn around to face the equator side of the sky (south from the northern hemisphere, north from the southern) and the same rotation looks different. Now the circles are so large that you only see their upper parts: stars come up along the eastern horizon, climb to their highest point as they cross the north–south line, and go down in the west. Facing south from the northern hemisphere that is left to right, clockwise; facing north from the southern hemisphere it is right to left.

Except on the equator, stars do not rise straight up. They climb on a slant, at 90° minus your latitude to the horizon (about 50° from mid-northern or mid-southern latitudes), leaning toward the equator side of the sky: to the right in the northern hemisphere, to the left in the southern. They set on the same slant in the west.
The Sun, the Moon and the planets share this daily turn. Their own slower movements against the stars come later in the course.

demo.title: Facing the equator side, east and west

steps.caption: From mid-northern latitudes (41°N), facing south at 8 pm in January, half an hour per second. Stars move left to right. The dotted arc is the whole night of Sirius: up in the southeast, highest due south around 11 pm, down in the southwest before dawn.
The same evening from mid-southern latitudes (34°S), facing north. Now the stars move right to left, and Sirius climbs almost overhead as it crosses due north around midnight (summer time there).

Facing east from mid-northern latitudes. Stars come up slanting to the right; the dots follow Regulus for five hours after it rises. On this date in 2027 the two bright extra lights rising with Regulus are Jupiter and Mars: planets ride the daily turn too.

Facing west at 9 pm. Everything sinks toward the horizon on a slant: down and to the right from the northern hemisphere, down and to the left from the southern. The half-lit Moon is going down with the stars: it shares the same daily motion.

sections.tryIt: Tonight, line up a bright star with the edge of a building or a rooftop antenna, standing in a spot you can find again. Come back to exactly that spot 20 minutes later. The star will have moved 5°, about three finger-widths at arm's length, and the direction it moved tells you where you are looking: up in the east, sideways toward the equator side of the sky (rightward facing south in the northern hemisphere, leftward facing north in the southern), down in the west.

figures.caption: Each line is one star's daily path; the dots are an hour apart. Facing east, stars climb out of the horizon on a slant of 90° minus your latitude. Switch to South to see the same paths peak, and try other latitudes to watch the slant change.

check.prompt: From latitude 35° N you watch a star rise due east. At what angle to the horizon does it climb?
choices: 90°, straight up
15°, one hour's turn
check.explanation: Stars rise at 90° minus your latitude: 90 − 35 = 55°. Only on the equator do they rise straight up; try it with the latitude slider in the figure.

keyPoints: The whole sky turns as one piece because Earth spins; the constellations keep their shapes.
The turn is 15° per hour: about a fist and a half at arm's length.
Stars circle the visible celestial pole: counter-clockwise around Polaris facing north in the northern hemisphere, clockwise around the south celestial pole facing south in the southern.
Stars rise in the east, are highest when they cross the north–south line, and set in the west, on a slant set by your latitude.

questions.prompt: Seen from the northern hemisphere, a star is due south at 9 pm. Roughly where will it be at 11 pm?
choices: About 30° farther west (to the right), a little lower
About 30° farther east (to the left), a little lower
In the same place: only planets move
About 15° higher, still due south
questions.explanation: The sky turns 15° per hour, east to west, so in two hours the star has moved about 30° to the right and started to sink from its highest point.

questions.prompt: Why does Polaris appear to stay still all night?
choices: It is the closest star to Earth
It is so far away that it cannot be seen to move
It lies almost exactly above Earth's axis of rotation
It moves, but too slowly because it is so bright
questions.explanation: Polaris sits less than 1° from the north celestial pole, the pivot of the turning sky, so its nightly circle is too small to notice.

questions.prompt: From the northern hemisphere you face north and watch the Big Dipper for several hours. Which way does it move?
choices: Clockwise around Polaris
Counter-clockwise around Polaris
Straight down toward the horizon
Left to right in a straight line
questions.explanation: Facing north, the sky turns counter-clockwise around the pole. Facing south, the same rotation looks like left-to-right motion. (From the southern hemisphere, facing south, the sky turns clockwise around the south celestial pole.)

questions.prompt: What actually causes the nightly motion of the stars?
choices: The stars orbit the Earth once a day
Earth travels around the Sun
The Moon's pull drags the sky around
Earth rotates on its axis once a day
questions.explanation: Earth spins west to east once a day, so the sky appears to turn east to west. Earth's orbit around the Sun causes the slower seasonal shift.

questions.prompt: A star rises at 7 pm. About how far has it travelled along its path by 10 pm?
questions.explanation: Three hours at 15° per hour is 45°, about four and a half fists at arm's length.
